q-11637:
- First, we check whether $CD=DC={I}_{2}.$ Computing $CD$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}CD & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, computing $DC$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}DC & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, statement I is true. As a result, $D={C}^{-1}$ and statement III is true too.

- Now, we check whether $DE=ED={I}_{2}.$ Computing $DE$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}DE & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ -2 & ∗\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne {I}_{2}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, statement II is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

q-102674:
- First, we check whether $AB=BA={I}_{2}.$ Computing $AB$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, computing $BA$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}BA & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, statement I is true. As a result, $B={A}^{-1}$ and statement III is true.

- Now, we check whether $AC=CA={I}_{2}.$ Computing $AC$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}∗ & -5 \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne {I}_{2}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, statement II is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

So, statement I is false. As a result, $A\ne {B}^{-1}$ and statement III is false too.

q-128491:
Remember that a square matrix is singular if its determinant is equal to $0.$

Using the formula, we take the alternating sum of the entries in the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(S) & =|\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{7} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ -\sqrt{7} & 2 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\sqrt{7}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7} & 0 \\ 5 & \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}|+\frac{1}{2}|\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{7} & 2 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\sqrt{7}(2\sqrt{7}-0)-0+\frac{1}{2}(0-10) \\  & =2\sqrt{7}\cdot 2\sqrt{7}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-10) \\  & =28-5 \\  & =23\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(S)=23\ne 0$, the matrix is **not ** singular. 

Therefore, only statement II is true.
